questionText:

Gandhiji on the Indian Elite

When his turn came to speak, Gandhiji charged the Indian elite with a lack of concern for the labouring poor. The opening of the BHU, he said, was “certainly a most gorgeous show”. But he worried about the contrast between the “richly bedecked noblemen” present and “millions of the poor” Indians who were absent. Gandhiji told the privileged invitees that “there is no salvation for India unless you strip yourself of this jewellery and hold it in trust for your countrymen in India.” “There can be no much spirit of self-government about us,” he went on, “if we take away or allow others to take away from them almost the whole of the results of their labour. Our salvation can only come through the farmer. Neither the lawyers, nor the doctors, nor the rich landlords are going to secure it.” Gandhiji’s speech at Banaras in February 1916 was, at one level, merely a statement of fact – namely, that Indian nationalism was an elite phenomenon, a creation of lawyers and doctors and landlords.

questionText:

"On 15 August 1947, as festivities erupted in New Delhi to celebrate Indian independence, Mahatma Gandhi was in Calcutta, staying in an abandoned Muslim mansion (Hydari Mansion in Beliaghata). Riots had convulsed Bengal since the Great Calcutta Killings of August 1946. Gandhi walked barefoot from village to village in Noakhali and fasted in Calcutta, dousing the fires of communal hatred. Admiring his moral courage, Viceroy Lord Mountbatten wrote to him: 'In the Punjab we have 55,000 soldiers and large-scale riots on our hands; in Bengal our force consists of one man, and there is no rioting.
